add_nodes.title: Ship heat shield turned around in three days
add_nodes.description: One Starship-class ship reaches 20 orbital flights and, at least once, flies twice within 72 hours, with heat-shield inspection and tile work done at the launch site. Achieved when flight records or the operator show both.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No ship has been caught or reflown: Flight 14 reached orbit on 28 Sep 2026 and splashed down. Musk expects the first ship and booster reflights at the end of 2026 or more likely early 2027. Mach33's base case has 18 flights per stack in 2030 and assumes later-generation stacks average 60 flights; Falcon 9 boosters that entered service in 2020 averaged 24 flights (Mach33, Sep 2026). Starfactory already uses specialized robots to install tiles and heat-shield pins (NASASpaceflight, Jan and Mar 2026).
add_nodes.pathway: P7 (exogenous launch clock; AI-math effect through damage and inspection models, P1->P6)
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Reuse at the scale of the launch clock (hundreds of heavy flights a year by the mid-2030s, about $13/kg internal cost in Mach33's base case) favors ships that turn around in days. Chain (S2): five reflights with two-week heat-shield turnaround (hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield, 2030) -> inspect-by-exception from tile damage and fleet heating models (2029-31) -> pad-side refurbishment with under 1% of tiles replaced per flight -> a ship flies twice within 72 hours and reaches 20 flights, about 2034. Once the material holds, the binding step is labor: imaging, tile removal and bonding, and checkout. AI mathematics shortens the inspection list; general-purpose robots shorten the work. S3 is a year ahead of S2 on the launch clock. S4 gets one more year: SpaceX is a robot-first firm, robots inspect and refurbish rockets from about 2029 in S4 (robo-launch-refurb), and process requalification takes 6-24 months, so S4 lands in 2032 against 2033 in S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: The economics may never need a 72-hour ship turnaround, because a larger fleet flying every few weeks gives the same cadence, so SpaceX may not try. If the ceramic tile concept is a dead end for rapid reuse, a new heat-shield architecture resets the clock by years.
add_nodes.signpost: Flight records showing one ship launched twice within a week, then within 72 hours; SpaceX statements on tiles replaced per flight and on robotic tile work at the pad.
add_nodes.note_2035: This is the 2032-35 step of Starship heat-shield reuse. S4 is a year ahead of S3 because tile inspection and replacement are labor-bound work that robots take over at SpaceX from about 2031, after requalification.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon. Spine extension (hard edge from hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield). The branch's one S4 year credit, under the four-condition rule: labor-bound refurbishment at a robot-first firm, robots useful there from 2029-31, prerequisite lands 2029, general-purpose robots beyond the specialized production tile installers already counted.

add_nodes.title: AI-designed heat-shield material in regular service
add_nodes.description: An AI-designed TPS material, coating or ablator (as defined in materials-tps-new-material-flight) is the baseline material for a primary heat-shield zone (forebody, nose or windward acreage) of an operational reentry vehicle and has flown at least 3 missions in that role. Coupons and test tiles do not count.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No AI-designed TPS material has flown, even as a coupon (general). Varda makes its C-PICA heat shields in-house and lost W-4 on reentry in May 2026; W-6 flew Sandia material samples and NASA Ames instrumented tiles. Starship Flight 10 (Aug 2025) flew metallic and actively cooled test tiles. New U.S. arc-jet capacity is being built (Kratos Project Helios, 20-25 MW, awarded Oct 2025).
add_nodes.why: Chain (S2): the first AI-designed coupon flies (materials-tps-new-material-flight, 2030) -> arc-jet qualification of the full material with its bond and attachment (1-2 years; the arc-jet queue binds) -> production scale-up and lot acceptance -> baseline on a commercial capsule or a reusable vehicle's windward zone -> three missions, about 2033. Uncrewed commercial operators need no certifier, which lifts the band above the P7 Speculative default; crewed use would be capped at Medium. S3 is a year earlier because closed-loop labs deliver qualified candidates sooner. S4 equals S3: robots speed specimen preparation, but arc-jet time and flight heritage at a small operator bind, worth under half a year.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Operators rarely change primary heat-shield materials, and after the W-4 loss and Artemis I's char loss they favor flight heritage. Gains from a new material may be small next to manufacturing, bonding and attachment.
add_nodes.signpost: A capsule maker or reusable-vehicle operator names an AI-designed material as the baseline for a primary heat-shield zone; arc-jet qualification reports for such a material.
add_nodes.note_2035: This extends the AI-material chain from a coupon to regular service in 2032-35. S4 equals S3 because arc-jet time and flight heritage bind at small operators, and robotic specimen work is worth under half a year.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: First aerocapture into orbit around another planet
add_nodes.description: A funded spacecraft (science, relay or commercial) enters orbit around Mars, Venus or Titan with a single atmospheric pass as its planned orbit-insertion method. Earth demonstrations do not count.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Aerocapture has never flown. NASA ordered a $350k study of an Arc-based Earth aerocapture demonstration from Inversion (11 Sep 2026, to 30 Jun 2027). Uranus studies find MSL-heritage aeroshells adequate for aerocapture (NTRS 20240014677). Mars launch windows open about Apr 2033 and mid-2035.
add_nodes.why: Chain (S2): an Earth aerocapture demonstration (hyper-aerocapture-demo, 2030 at the earliest, Medium by 2035) -> a small Mars or Venus mission adopts aerocapture to save insertion propellant (2-3 year build) -> launch in a window (Mars about Apr 2033 or mid-2035) -> capture on arrival, about 2034. AI makes guidance, dispersion and rarefied-flow analysis cheap, so a small team can carry the analysis load; funding and the demo's success bind. Above the P7 Speculative default in S2-S4 only because cheap launch and cheap analysis put such a mission within a commercial or small agency budget. S4 equals S3 because capital and launch windows bind.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: After a demo, a first planetary use still needs a mission whose design closes only with aerocapture, and with cheap launch most small missions can carry extra propellant instead.
add_nodes.signpost: A Mars or Venus mission selection, or a commercial Mars relay, that baselines aerocapture for orbit insertion.
add_nodes.note_2035: The first planetary use follows an Earth demo by a mission build and a launch window, so it falls in 2033-35 at the earliest. Capital and windows bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: Second heavy Mars lander touches down near the first
add_nodes.description: A second lander of 20 t or more lands intact on Mars within 1 km of an earlier lander, without disabling damage to it from plume or ejecta. This is the precision an outpost cargo build-up needs.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No 20 t-class Mars landing has been attempted. Landing ellipses for Curiosity and Perseverance were about 20 x 7 km and 8 x 7 km (general). Apollo 12 landed about 160 m from Surveyor 3, and its exhaust sandblasted the probe (general). In Feb 2026 SpaceX put Mars about 5-7 years out behind a Moon-first priority.
add_nodes.pathway: P7 (launch windows; AI-math effect through guidance and plume-surface models)
add_nodes.why: Chain: first heavy landing (hyper-mars-heavy-landing, 2031 window at the earliest) -> site data and terrain-relative navigation from that flight -> a second ship targets the same site in the Apr 2033 window and arrives late 2033. Several ships in one window could also do it. Landing within 1 km needs guidance with proven convergence and plume-surface models that bound ejecta damage; AI mathematics helps both, while windows and the first landing gate the date. The band is the first landing's chance by 2035 (Medium) times the chance a second ship lands close, so Low; it sits above the P7 default because SpaceX plans several ships per window. S4 equals S3 because orbital mechanics binds.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics barely changes the date; windows and SpaceX's priorities decide it. SpaceX may also spread early landings across sites to scout, which delays a close second landing.
add_nodes.signpost: A SpaceX statement that a second Mars ship will target the first ship's site; published plume-ejecta keep-out distances for Starship-class landers.
add_nodes.note_2035: This is the 2033-window follow-on to the first heavy landing. Windows bind, so every scenario shares the year and S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: Rocket cargo as a regular military logistics service
add_nodes.description: Point-to-point rocket deliveries of 30 t or more reach 10 or more in one year as an operational U.S. military logistics service, with recovered vehicles and at least two approved remote landing sites. Demonstration flights do not count.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: AFRL awarded SpaceX a $102M, 5-year Rocket Cargo contract in 2022; the program goal is ~100 short tons anywhere within an hour. The Johnston Atoll environmental assessment (up to 10 landings a year) was suspended in July 2025. No demonstration as of Oct 2026.
add_nodes.pathway: P7 (regulatory and DoD clock; AI-math effect marginal)
add_nodes.why: Chain (S2): three demonstration flights (hyper-p2p-cargo-demo, 2031) -> a program of record and budget line -> environmental assessments and host-nation agreements for at least two landing sites (2-3 years) -> 10+ deliveries in one year, about 2034. Cheap, frequent Starship flights make each delivery affordable, but site approvals, overflight rules and DoD budgets set the date. AI mathematics has essentially no effect. Rated above the P7 default in S2-S4 because a funded program and a contractor exist. S4 equals S3 because regulation binds.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Airlift is cheaper for almost every load, and DoD may keep rocket cargo as a demonstrated capability that it rarely uses. Remote landing sites face environmental and diplomatic objections.
add_nodes.signpost: A Rocket Cargo program of record in a DoD budget request; a second approved landing site.
add_nodes.note_2035: This turns the point-to-point demo into a service in 2033-35 at the earliest. Regulation and budgets bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: A crewed vehicle flies a heat shield sized by probabilistic margins
add_nodes.description: A crewed reentry vehicle certified by NASA or another space agency flies a heat shield whose thickness was set to a reliability target with joint probabilistic margins, including a flight-calibrated model-form term, in place of stacked aerothermal factors.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: NASA practice stacks deterministic aerothermal factors and combines branches by root-sum-square (SRL design, IPPW 2026); the SRL alternative-margining study was preliminary, and SRL ended when Mars Sample Return received no FY2026 funding. Artemis I's char loss pushed NASA toward more margin; Artemis II flew a modified entry on the same shield design (10 Apr 2026).
add_nodes.why: Chain (S2): probabilistic sizing adopted on uncrewed vehicles (2029) -> flight-calibrated model-form bounds (2030) -> an agency margin policy that allows reliability-based sizing for crew (2031-32) -> a heat-shield block change on a crewed capsule (Orion, Dragon or a national crew vehicle) -> flight, about 2034. The certifier must accept the method, so the band is capped at Medium, and after Artemis I crewed programs favor margin, which holds S2-S4 at Low by 2035. S1 lacks the calibrated bounds in time. S4 equals S3 because institutions bind.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Crewed programs rarely trade heat-shield margin for mass, and a thinner crewed shield saves little that matters. Agencies may use the method for analysis while keeping stacked factors for sizing.
add_nodes.signpost: A NASA EDL or TPS margin-policy revision that allows reliability-based sizing for crewed vehicles; a crewed heat-shield redesign that cites it.
add_nodes.note_2035: This is where the margin chain meets crewed risk posture, in 2033-35 at the earliest. Certifier acceptance binds, so S4 equals S3 and no scenario rises above Low by 2035.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-entry (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon. Regulatory cap Medium; no named mechanism for crewed TPS margins is in motion, so 2035 stays capped.

patch.thesis: AI uncertainty analysis lets commercial capsules fly thinner heat shields around 2030 (base case, Medium). Ship heat shields reach five reflights by 2030 and three-day turnaround around 2034. Mars landings, aerocapture and crewed use wait on windows, budgets and regulators. Robots (S4) save a year only on tile work.
